author: BrentDesk Research
headline: Kyrgyz Republic presents Tamchy financial territory at AIM Congress
deck: The Kyrgyz Republic presented its Tamchy special financial investment territory at AIM Congress without attaching values or agreements.
excerpt: The Kyrgyz Republic presented the Tamchy Special Financial Investment Territory at AIM Congress in Dubai as a Central Asian gateway, without disclosed investment values.
content:
Among the country presentations at AIM Congress, which closed at Dubai World Trade Centre on 9 September, the Kyrgyz Republic presented its Tamchy Special Financial Investment Territory as a gateway to Central Asia for foreign capital, with Ayaz Baetov, chairman of the management council, leading the presentation.

No investment values, agreements or committed projects were attached to it, which places it in the same category as most of what this congress produced. That is worth stating rather than glossing.

The proposition itself is coherent. Special economic and financial zones are a standard instrument for jurisdictions seeking to attract capital they cannot attract through their general legal and regulatory environment. The zone offers defined rules, tax treatment, dispute resolution and often a separate regulator, ring-fenced from the wider system. The Gulf knows the model well: the Dubai International Financial Centre and Abu Dhabi Global Market are the regional examples, and both have succeeded in attracting institutions that would not otherwise have located there.

Central Asia's interest in Gulf capital is straightforward. The region has infrastructure requirements, mineral resources and a location between China, Russia, Iran and South Asia that makes it strategically interesting and commercially complicated. Gulf sovereign funds have been diversifying geographically, and Central Asia offers exposure that is neither Western developed markets nor the African and South Asian destinations already well covered.

For a publication concerned with the physical economy the relevant question is what such a zone would actually build. Financial zones attract financial institutions; they do not by themselves produce infrastructure, manufacturing or logistics capacity. The mechanism by which a special financial territory converts into physical investment runs through the projects it finances, and none were named.

The wider congress context is one of scale without disclosed specifics. The event ran under the patronage of Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum with Thani bin Ahmed Al Zeyoudi, UAE Minister of State for Foreign Trade, Mohammad Ali Rashed Lootah of Dubai Chambers and Jasem Al-Budaiwi, Secretary General of the GCC, among those attending. Ras Al Khaimah promoted a base of more than 73,000 registered companies.

No closing communiqué, foreign direct investment announcement carrying a value, or memorandum with named parties had been published as the congress closed. A widely reported attendance figure of 15,831 participants from 181 countries matches the 2025 edition's published result exactly and should be treated as prior-year carry-over. For Gulf investors the question a zone has to answer is what it finances, and Tamchy has not yet answered it publicly. Until a special financial territory names the projects it intends to fund, a presentation of this kind is a statement of availability rather than of pipeline, and Gulf sovereign investors have seen a great many of those.
